The textile is finished by unworked warp threads.

physical.title: tunic
physical.summary: Man's cotton tunic, made of narrow strips of cloth, dyed dark brown and machine-stitched together. The tunic is straight, with wide short sleeves, side vents, rounded neck and slit opening at front. Hem of tunic has raw edge with tassels at intervals. Tunic decorated on front and back with narrow strips of metal in figurative designs. Front of tunic has square pocket on left; back has openwork net of twisted and dyed cotton thread, secured by metal strips to form lozenges attached at the midpoint.

cultural.vision_reason: The picture shows a hand-sewn, resist-dyed cotton cap with geometric decoration, tassels, and attached charm-like parcels. It is a plausible traditional garment made and used by Dogon people, with no evidence of a conflicting cultural tradition.

physical.title: cap
physical.summary: Cap: plain woven cotton. The hat consists of two oblongs of hemmed cotton completely (hand) sewn up along two joining edges. The other two sides are partially sewn up joining the corners of the sections previously mentioned leaving engough room for the head. Three of the hats corners have two cotton tassels attached. The original colour of the cotton was a red brown. The cotton was then redyed using the wax resist dyed technique in dark brown creating a geometric design. There are also a number of small reptile skin parcels (possibly charms) attached using leather thongs.

cultural.vision_reason: The image shows a dark indigo, resist-dyed handwoven wrapper with repeated blue stitch patterns, consistent with Dogon textile production. It fits the claimed ethnicity and textile category.

physical.title: textile; wrapper
physical.summary: Cloth (probably a wrapper) formed of 7 strips of hand-spun white cotton, hand-sewn together along the selvedges. After assembling, the whole cloth has been stitch-tied with repeated blocks of three lines of chevrons, arranged regularly along each strip. The two outer strips have only a single block of chevrons; the five strips in the centre have two lines. The blocks are arranged to form bands across the cloth. The cloth has been dyed twice, once when stitched, and again after unstitching over the whole cloth. Along one end of the cloth is an extra pattern of two crosses on each strip.

cultural.vision_reason: The picture shows a handwoven indigo cloth or skirt with embroidered geometric patterns and fringed ends, a traditional textile plausibly made and used by Dogon people. It fits the claimed ethnicity and garment category.

physical.title: cloth; skirt
physical.summary: Cloth/skirt composed of 7 narrow strips hand-sewn together along the selvedges. The cloth is hand-woven from hand-spun cotton used in both warp and weft that has been dyed a uniform shade of indigo. One strip has been left undecorated, while the other six, after being sewn together, have been hand-embroidered using imported European thread coloured red, yellow and blue, with patterns of diamonds, square boxes and zig-zag lines that run across the cloth. At both ends there is a long fringe of indigo tassels which appear to have been braided from the loose warp ends.

cultural.vision_reason: The image shows a strip-woven, indigo stitch-resist dyed cotton skirt with the characteristic Dogon triangle-and-bar pattern, and the museum explicitly credits Dogon makers; this matches known Dogon women's dress.

physical.title: skirt
physical.summary:
Cotton woven indigo dyed skirt. Made of seven (7) narrow strips hand-woven and hand-sewn together selvedge to selvedge. The central strip is narrower than the others. The ends of the strips are finished with a hem. 

The piece had been manually stitch-resist indigo dyed after weaving. It is decorated with bars and squares which together form six groups of warp-facing triangles. On the central strip is the inscription "L'enfant vos [vaut] mieux que l'argent."
